title: Independent arithmetic verification
connection: Check generated triples by two algebraically distinct routes: cleared products and reduced rational sums.
why: Independent formulations can catch implementation errors or malformed records.
first_step: Write a small verifier specification and test it against deliberately corrupted triples.

title: Trusted-kernel pipelines
connection: Route heuristic discoveries into a tiny theorem-checking kernel rather than trusting the search or symbolic algebra package.
why: The proof obligation stays explicit even when discovery uses complicated tools.
first_step: Choose one elementary family and separate its discovery script from a minimal proof of the resulting identity and divisibility conditions.

title: Grammar compression of certificates
connection: Compress a finite certificate database using shared identity templates and parameter substitutions.
why: A short grammar can reveal repeated constructions hidden among many individual triples.
first_step: Cluster exact triples by common rational-expression templates and compare compressed description lengths.

title: Algorithmic simplicity of difficult instances
connection: Compare the shortest known certificate-generating program with the smallest numerical certificate.
why: A huge denominator might still have a simple recurrence description, suggesting a different notion of difficulty.
first_step: For a small set of large-height examples, search short recurrences generating their denominator triples.

title: Minimum-description-length family selection
connection: Balance the coverage of a formula against the complexity of its exceptional-case conditions.
why: This discourages overfitting while keeping every mathematically valid family available.
first_step: Encode formula syntax and residue exceptions with an explicit code, then compare several portfolios on held-out primes.

title: Levin-style program search
connection: Dovetail candidate certificate programs with budgets depending on program length.
why: This gives a systematic discovery baseline and highlights the cost of the chosen expression language.
first_step: Enumerate a tiny arithmetic-program language and allocate execution steps by a prefix-code weight.

title: Fair interleaving of infinite families
connection: Run countably many valid parameter searches in a schedule that eventually explores every finite parameter tuple.
why: Fairness prevents one expensive family from starving other methods, without guaranteeing ES itself.
first_step: Specify a diagonal schedule over family index and parameter height and prove every finite tuple is reached.

title: Stopping bounds for ordered triples
connection: Exploit x≤y≤z to derive finite search bounds for fixed p before discussing algorithmic completeness.
why: A correct finite bound distinguishes exhaustive verification from an arbitrary cutoff.
first_step: Derive p/4<x≤3p/4 and the resulting bound on y from the positive residual, then implement a bounded enumeration plan.

title: Total-search complexity questions
connection: Ask what complexity classification would follow if ES witnesses had a specified polynomial bit-length bound.
why: The conditional formulation separates existence from efficient verification and avoids assuming ES is already a total search theorem.
first_step: Write the witness relation and identify exactly which unproved size and existence statements are needed for a TFNP-style classification.

title: Parameterized complexity by factor count
connection: Treat the number of distinct auxiliary prime factors or modulus structure as an algorithmic parameter.
why: Subset-product search may be tractable in a parameter even when the integer itself is large.
first_step: Derive running-time bounds for residue selection in terms of factor count and group invariant factors.

title: Treewidth of arithmetic factor graphs
connection: Measure the width of a factor graph after separating valuations, carries, and residues.
why: Small treewidth would support exact dynamic programming for that bounded encoding.
first_step: Construct three alternative factor graphs for the same tiny instance and compare elimination widths.

title: Meet-in-the-middle divisor selection
connection: Split prime-power factors into two groups and match complementary target residues.
why: This is an exact algorithmic alternative to enumerating every divisor when modular inverses are handled correctly.
first_step: Implement the split for unit factors of a small auxiliary integer and handle nonunits in separate valuation strata.

title: FFT convolution on cyclic residue coordinates
connection: Use discrete-log coordinates in a cyclic unit group to turn divisor-selection convolution into cyclic convolution.
why: Fast convolution can count residue witnesses exactly with suitable integer reconstruction.
first_step: For a small prime modulus, compare direct dynamic programming with an exact convolution implementation.

title: Bitset propagation of attainable residues
connection: Represent reachable residues by bitsets and update them under each allowed factor power.
why: Bit-parallel operations can make large bounded surveys cheaper without changing the mathematics.
first_step: Benchmark bitset and set-based reachability for moduli below 1000 using the same factorizations.

title: Decision diagrams for factor subsets
connection: Compress repeated residual subproblems using zero-suppressed decision diagrams or related shared DAGs.
why: Many distinct divisors can share the same remaining residue problem.
first_step: Build a small decision diagram for target-residue divisor selection and compare its node count with the number of divisors.

title: Dominance pruning of partial certificates
connection: Define a sound partial-order dominance relation between search states with identical arithmetic obligations.
why: A dominated state can be removed only when every completion has a no-more-expensive counterpart.
first_step: Prove one dominance rule based on equal residue state and remaining factor inventory, then measure pruning.

title: Modular fingerprints for duplicate detection
connection: Use several modular reductions to cheaply reject unequal symbolic or numerical certificates before exact comparison.
why: Fingerprints accelerate deduplication while exact fallback prevents collisions from becoming false identities.
first_step: Design a hash-plus-exact-check pipeline for canonical denominator triples and rational identity expressions.

title: Arithmetic-circuit complexity
connection: Compare expanded polynomial identities with compact straight-line arithmetic circuits.
why: A low-complexity circuit may expose composition structure that expansion obscures.
first_step: Represent three candidate families as circuits and count multiplication gates after common-subexpression elimination.

title: Straight-line certificates for huge denominators
connection: Store denominators by exact arithmetic programs when their decimal expansions are unwieldy.
why: Compact descriptions can make recurrent or compositional families practical, provided equality is still verified exactly.
first_step: Encode a small recurrence family as straight-line programs and compare evaluation and verification costs.

title: Modular interpolation of identities
connection: Recover candidate polynomial coefficients from evaluations modulo several primes and reconstruct rational coefficients.
why: This can make symbolic discovery cheaper, followed by exact identity checking.
first_step: Recover a known low-degree numerator identity from modular samples as a pipeline sanity check.

title: Sparse interpolation of parameter relations
connection: Exploit a small expected monomial support when reconstructing relations among certificate parameters.
why: Sparse reconstruction may discover concise algebraic constraints missed by dense fitting.
first_step: Use a low-degree monomial dictionary on a sample of exact certificates and validate any recovered relation symbolically.

title: Polynomial identity testing with deterministic closure
connection: Use randomized evaluations to reject false formulas quickly, then perform exact symbolic verification on survivors.
why: Random testing is a filter, never the final proof of an identity.
first_step: Generate a batch of candidate identities, filter at random integer points, and expand only the survivors.

title: Small-root lattice attacks on residual equations
connection: Check whether a chosen ES parametrization yields a modular polynomial with a genuinely small unknown suitable for lattice small-root methods.
why: Cryptanalytic techniques are relevant only when explicit size inequalities are met.
first_step: Derive one univariate modular residual and check whether a Coppersmith theorem covers its degree, modulus, and root bound.

title: Approximate common divisors as hints
connection: Explore cases where several auxiliary values are near multiples of an unknown useful factor.
why: Shared approximate divisibility might reveal a factor-selection strategy if the error model is justified.
first_step: Construct exact small examples from known certificates and test whether the useful factor is recoverable from the proposed hints.

title: Hidden-number-style parameter recovery
connection: Treat partial information about modular products as a lattice recovery problem for an auxiliary parameter.
why: The analogy is meaningful only when the available information matches an explicit hidden-number instance.
first_step: Write a toy recovery problem with exact known high bits and compare its recovered parameters with valid certificates.

title: Partial factor bits from congruence constraints
connection: Use the required residue of a useful divisor as partial information in a factorization problem.
why: A residue class supplies genuine bits of structure, though it may be far too weak for existing algorithms.
first_step: For small auxiliary integers, measure how much the target congruence shrinks the divisor search and check partial-factor recovery literature.

title: Smooth-order factorization steering
connection: Choose auxiliary parameters whose likely useful factors have smooth multiplicative-group order, then test a p−1-style factoring strategy.
why: This is a construction-and-search heuristic, not a claim that such factors always exist.
first_step: For C≤100, compare certificate usefulness of factors found cheaply by a small smooth-order budget.

title: Elliptic-curve factorization as a probe
connection: Use small factoring budgets to sample auxiliary factors and ask whether easily found factors already yield many certificates.
why: This measures whether complete factorization is unnecessary for exploratory coverage.
first_step: Apply equal small ECM budgets to a bounded list of auxiliary values and verify all certificates obtained from partial factorizations.

title: Batch gcd across parameter values
connection: Compute shared factors among many p-tied auxiliary integers using gcd relations and batch techniques.
why: Shared factors can be extracted without factoring every value separately.
first_step: For fixed p and bounded C, derive pairwise gcd restrictions and compare batch extraction with individual trial division.

title: Product and remainder trees
connection: Use product trees to test many candidate divisors against many auxiliary values efficiently.
why: This supports broad experiments and may reveal unexpectedly reusable factors.
first_step: Design a memory-bounded remainder-tree pass for a small family of auxiliary values and target divisors.

title: Factor-base relations for certificate search
connection: Collect auxiliary values smooth over a chosen factor base and record their residue-selection structure.
why: This borrows a relation-collection viewpoint without assuming factorization-style linear algebra directly solves ES.
first_step: Build a tiny factor-base relation matrix and determine what additional condition turns a relation into an actual target divisor.

title: Discrete-log coordinates with multiplicity constraints
connection: Use discrete logs only to linearize residues, retaining the bounded exponent ranges of actual divisors.
why: Solving the unrestricted linear congruence alone would create nonexistent divisors; bounded coefficients are essential.
first_step: Compare bounded and unrestricted exponent solutions in a small cyclic unit group and quantify spurious solutions.

title: Factoring-free gcd certificates
connection: Search for constructions where a useful divisor is produced as a gcd of two explicit expressions.
why: A gcd can supply a verified factor without requiring complete factorization.
first_step: Try short polynomial gcd expressions in p and C and retain only cases where the gcd provably has the target residue.

title: Certified prime selection for experiments
connection: Separate primality verification of test inputs from ES witness verification so arithmetic strata remain trustworthy.
why: Misclassified inputs could distort experiments about prime-only behavior.
first_step: Specify a test-data format carrying primality evidence or a reproducible deterministic primality procedure alongside each p.

title: Las Vegas certificate discovery
connection: Allow random candidate generation but accept outputs only after deterministic exact verification.
why: Randomness then affects runtime rather than the correctness of reported witnesses.
first_step: Design a randomized parameter sampler with explicit timeouts and an independent certificate checker.

title: Small-bias parameter schedules
connection: Replace unrestricted random residues with a small explicitly generated sample space and measure which character tests it fools.
why: A derandomized schedule may preserve relevant coverage statistics if the test class is identified.
first_step: Construct a tiny small-bias distribution for a selected finite group and compare its character averages with those of uniform sampling.

title: Perfect-hash-style family isolation
connection: Use hash partitions to isolate one witness among many candidate factors, simplifying a bounded search subproblem.
why: Isolation can aid algorithm design, while an exact check prevents the hash mechanism from inventing witnesses.
first_step: Apply a small family of residue hashes to known multi-witness instances and measure isolation rates.

title: Memory-bounded parallel parameter search
connection: Split the auxiliary domain into deterministic chunks with no shared giant divisor table.
why: A streaming design enables much broader evidence collection without uncontrolled Cartesian-product allocations.
first_step: Specify chunk sizes, per-worker memory caps, and an exact merge key for a bounded search prototype.

title: Cache keys as mathematical assumptions
connection: Key cached computations by the full parametrization, modulus, positivity convention, and search bounds.
why: This prevents results from one mathematical model being silently reused in a different one.
first_step: Audit a toy search cache and construct two deliberately incompatible configurations that must not share entries.

title: Permutation-equivariant certificate models
connection: Train predictors on unordered denominator triples using features invariant under all six coordinate permutations.
why: Respecting exact symmetry can reduce spurious distinctions in learned family structure.
first_step: Compare a symmetric feature model with a raw-coordinate baseline on canonicalized bounded certificates.

title: Factor-graph neural heuristics
connection: Use a graph model whose nodes represent prime factors, residues, and valuation slots to rank partial assignments.
why: The architecture mirrors actual arithmetic constraints, while final outputs still require exact verification.
first_step: Train only on tiny exhaustively solved factor-selection instances and test ranking quality on larger held-out ones.

title: Learning the next family to try
connection: Predict which exact certificate family should be attempted first from cheap features of p.
why: A learned selector accelerates search without becoming part of the correctness argument.
first_step: Compare a small classifier with a fixed family order using measured total arithmetic operations.

title: Decision trees as conjecture extractors
connection: Fit shallow trees using residue and character features, then translate each leaf into a proposed arithmetic lemma.
why: A transparent leaf condition is a concrete object for proof or counterexample search.
first_step: Fit a depth-three tree for one family's success and exhaustively test each leaf condition in a larger range.

title: Symbolic regression of witness costs
connection: Fit simple formulas for least auxiliary size using arithmetic features rather than raw prime magnitude alone.
why: The goal is a testable growth conjecture or selector, not numerical evidence of universal existence.
first_step: Restrict symbolic regression to a small grammar and validate predictions on a disjoint prime range.

title: Rational-function recognition in families
connection: Group certificates by a discrete template label and attempt exact rational interpolation of their parameters as functions of p.
why: Recovered formulas can be verified symbolically and their integrality domains derived.
first_step: For one visually coherent cluster, interpolate low-degree rational functions from exact data and test unused points.

title: Counterfactual feature interventions
connection: Alter one arithmetic feature in synthetic parameter data while holding the exact algebraic model fixed where possible.
why: This helps distinguish genuine mechanisms from correlated labels in observational prime data.
first_step: Within one residue-compatible family, vary a single auxiliary prime factor and measure the resulting target-residue change.

title: Active learning at family boundaries
connection: Choose new examples near the boundary where a simple family selector changes its prediction.
why: Boundary cases may expose missing congruence hypotheses more quickly than uniform sampling.
first_step: Train a shallow selector, query its most ambiguous bounded inputs, and inspect the exact divisibility reasons for each outcome.

title: Uncertainty-guided experiment allocation
connection: Allocate computation to prime strata where count models disagree rather than only to predicted hardest cases.
why: Disagreement can expose model misspecification and broaden the exploratory dataset.
first_step: Compare two simple count models and search a balanced sample of their largest disagreement cases.

title: Calibration of success predictions
connection: Measure whether predicted success probabilities for a fixed search budget match observed frequencies.
why: Well-calibrated uncertainty is useful for scheduling, but cannot turn a probability estimate into a proof.
first_step: Build reliability curves on held-out primes and separate calibration by small-residue strata.

title: Out-of-distribution prime tests
connection: Train only on one range or residue stratum and evaluate on genuinely new arithmetic regimes.
why: This detects selectors that memorize local density patterns rather than generalizable mechanisms.
first_step: Hold out an entire congruence class and a larger magnitude range, reporting both separately.

title: Explaining count outliers
connection: For primes with unexpectedly few witnesses, decompose the prediction error into factorization, local-density, and family-overlap features.
why: An explanation may suggest a targeted new identity instead of merely another statistical model.
first_step: Select ten low-count outliers and compare each feature against matched primes of similar size.

title: Matched prime pairs
connection: Pair primes with nearly identical cheap arithmetic features but very different least witness costs.
why: Contrasts can isolate information missing from a proposed selector.
first_step: Match on residues modulo a small modulus and several character labels, then inspect auxiliary factorizations of the largest-cost contrasts.

title: Biclustering families and primes
connection: Find blocks of the incidence matrix where a group of families succeeds on a specific group of primes.
why: Blocks may correspond to hidden arithmetic regimes with complementary constructions.
first_step: Run a simple exact or heuristic biclustering on a bounded incidence matrix and characterize blocks by residue features.

title: Nonnegative latent mechanisms
connection: Factor a nonnegative count matrix into a few latent family and prime components, then seek arithmetic interpretations.
why: Unlike a proof, the factorization only suggests which mechanisms might be shared.
first_step: Fit ranks two through five and inspect whether components align with known gcd or character labels.

title: Embeddings of matrix words
connection: Learn or hand-design representations that place equivalent or easily transformable matrix words near each other.
why: A useful representation could guide discovery of short exact rewrite sequences.
first_step: Compare embeddings based on modular actions with raw word edit distance on verified equivalent words.

title: Motifs in proof graphs
connection: Mine repeated small subgraphs in graphs of exact algebraic derivations.
why: Recurring proof fragments may become reusable lemmas or identity-generation macros.
first_step: Encode ten elementary derivations as operation DAGs and identify repeated three-operation motifs.

title: Invariant discovery with counterexamples
connection: Search low-degree expressions constant under verified certificate transformations, rejecting candidates on fresh exact examples.
why: A discovered invariant can organize orbit structure and explain why some moves fail to connect families.
first_step: Solve linear equations for quadratic invariants of one transformation and check survivors symbolically.

title: Language-model analogy proposals with algebraic gates
connection: Use a language model only to propose cross-domain encodings, then require a written map and a checked toy instance.
why: The algebraic gate separates a useful analogy from merely similar terminology.
first_step: Prompt for five encodings of the same residual factor equation and discard only those lacking a well-defined map.

title: Semantic retrieval of equivalent equations
connection: Search literature by algebraic shape and alternate terminology rather than only by the phrase Erdős–Straus.
why: Relevant results may use norm equations, reciprocal partitions, or restricted divisor sums under different names.
first_step: Form five precise search queries from the equation (ay−b)(az−b)=b² and inspect the returned definitions.

title: Citation-graph bridges
connection: Trace papers that connect two relevant areas, such as restricted divisor problems and finite-group zero-sum theory.
why: Bridge papers may supply a transferable lemma not indexed under Egyptian fractions.
first_step: Search for a paper using both topic vocabularies, verify it exists, and inspect its cited technical tools.

title: A dictionary of incompatible conventions
connection: Translate denominator ordering, primitive conditions, and sign conventions across candidate papers before comparing results.
why: Apparent contradictions or missed equivalences can come from different definitions.
first_step: Build a one-page convention table for three verified sources once located, including exact theorem hypotheses.

title: Lean formalization of one family
connection: Formalize one elementary rational identity together with its positivity and divisibility hypotheses.
why: A small verified example establishes the shape of proof obligations without trying to formalize the whole campaign.
first_step: Choose the simplest directly checked family and locate the Lean lemmas needed for rational field simplification.

title: Positivity proof certificates
connection: Attach explicit positive-factor decompositions to every symbolic denominator expression.
why: An algebraically correct identity can still fail as an ES construction if denominators are nonpositive.
first_step: For three candidate formulas, rewrite each denominator into products or sums whose signs follow from stated hypotheses.

title: Integer–rational coercion discipline
connection: Treat exact division as a separate proved step before moving a parametrization from integers to rational identities.
why: This prevents silent truncation or unjustified integrality in machine and human proofs.
first_step: Write a typed proof outline for one formula, marking every use of integer divisibility and rational coercion.

title: A library of divisibility transport lemmas
connection: Collect reusable lemmas carrying divisibility through substitutions, gcd cancellation, and complementary factors.
why: These small facts recur across many distinct constructions and can reduce proof friction.
first_step: Formalize or precisely state five transport lemmas needed by the residual factor-pair equivalence.

title: Certified completeness of finite enumeration
connection: Prove the ordered-denominator bounds used by an exhaustive verifier and connect them to its loop limits.
why: A witness checker proves individual successes; a completeness proof also validates bounded absence claims.
first_step: Write a proof outline linking x and y inequalities to each loop endpoint of a toy exhaustive search.

title: Formal translation between word and fraction certificates
connection: Specify both sides of one short matrix-word equivalence and prove the conversion including sign and congruence conditions.
why: A checked bridge would allow discovery in one language and validation in another.
first_step: Select a length-two or length-three word and manually derive the forward and reverse formulas before formalizing.

title: Parametric proof objects
connection: Represent an infinite family by a polynomial identity proof plus a separate modular integrality proof.
why: This makes the difference between many tested examples and a genuine family theorem explicit.
first_step: Define a record containing symbolic denominators, domain hypotheses, the identity, and integrality certificates.

title: Replayable symbolic proof traces
connection: Export each algebraic simplification as a sequence of exact transformations rather than only a final yes/no answer.
why: A small checker can replay discovery-tool output independently.
first_step: For one rational identity, record clearing denominators, ring normalization, and hypothesis use as separate trace steps.

title: Extracting certificate algorithms from proofs
connection: Given a constructive family theorem, extract the parameter-to-denominator function with its domain test.
why: The extracted algorithm connects proof structure to measurable search behavior.
first_step: Take one hand-proved family and write its domain predicate and witness constructor as separate pure functions.

title: Property-based arithmetic testing
connection: Generate structured random inputs satisfying a family's hypotheses rather than arbitrary integers.
why: This efficiently catches transcription errors while remaining only a development check.
first_step: Design generators for divisibility-compatible parameters and test the cleared identity and positivity separately.

title: Metamorphic tests from scaling
connection: Use exact transformations such as scaling a valid triple along with n to generate consistency checks.
why: If 4/n=Σ1/x, scaling all four quantities by a positive integer preserves the identity.
first_step: Specify a test transforming a valid witness at n into one at kn and verify all fields update consistently.

title: Mutation testing for certificate checkers
connection: Deliberately change signs, residues, denominator values, and domain assumptions to test whether a verifier rejects false claims.
why: A checker that accepts corrupted data cannot support trustworthy experiments.
first_step: Create one mutation per required condition and confirm that each is rejected for a mathematical reason.

title: Croot-related exact-sum techniques
connection: Investigate whether methods in work associated with Croot on Egyptian fractions contain a tunable exact-sum or smooth-denominator ingredient.
why: A method for assembling reciprocal sums might have a restricted three-term component, but this is only a literature lead.
first_step: Check which Croot papers prove exact reciprocal-sum statements and extract the precise flexibility in numerator, length, and denominator support.

title: Erdős–Graham coloring methods
connection: Ask whether techniques around the Erdős–Graham Egyptian-fraction problem suggest a useful partition of denominator candidates.
why: Coloring or density arguments might inspire family selection even if their conclusions involve many terms.
first_step: Locate a verified statement and proof source, then check whether any intermediate lemma controls a fixed small number of terms.

title: Bloom-related density increments
connection: Investigate whether work associated with Bloom on unit-fraction problems offers a density-increment mechanism adaptable to structured divisor sets.
why: The potentially transferable object is a lemma about reciprocal mass, not an assumed three-term theorem.
first_step: Find the relevant paper, verify its hypotheses, and compare its denominator set with divisors of a p-tied integer.

title: Sylvester-style product recurrences
connection: Check how classical product recurrences for Egyptian fractions encode divisibility, then ask whether alternative initial conditions yield three-term terminal states.
why: Product recurrences provide exact rational identities whose length and congruences can be tracked.
first_step: Locate a reliable source for the recurrence, derive it independently, and test modified initial parameters symbolically.

title: Fibonacci–Sylvester greedy residuals
connection: Study the exact residual sequence of the greedy algorithm on 4/p and identify arithmetic conditions forcing termination within three terms.
why: This is a concrete subfamily selector even when greedy expansion takes longer in general.
first_step: Derive the first two greedy residual numerators in each p modulo 4 case and factor their denominators.

title: Engel expansions as intermediate representations
connection: Compare multiplicative-denominator Engel expansions of 4/p with ordinary unit-fraction decompositions and possible regroupings.
why: Nested denominator structure may make some exact merges easier to describe.
first_step: Compute short Engel expansions for small primes and test adjacent-term merges into a single unit fraction.

title: Lüroth-style digit systems
connection: Check whether a rational expansion with consecutive-product denominators can be converted into a useful three-term ES ansatz.
why: The digit system offers a different exact decomposition grammar, not an automatic short representation.
first_step: Verify the precise Lüroth expansion formula and test finite rational examples for algebraically valid regroupings.

title: Ostrowski numeration of parameter choices
connection: Use continued-fraction-based numeration to encode auxiliary integers relative to p and a chosen modulus.
why: The digits may align with Euclidean recurrences and make congruence repair more local.
first_step: For one rational rotation, write several successful auxiliary values in Ostrowski coordinates and compare their digit patterns.

title: Odd-denominator greedy variants
connection: Compare a greedy rule restricted to odd denominators with unrestricted greedy search on related residual fractions.
why: Restrictions can expose parity mechanisms even if they make termination harder.
first_step: Define a precise odd-denominator choice rule and compute its first three residuals on a bounded set of admissible rational inputs.

title: Primary-source identity genealogy
connection: Trace an elementary ES identity backward through citations to learn which substitutions and failed variants accompanied it.
why: Historical derivations may reveal nearby constructions omitted from modern summaries.
first_step: Choose one commonly reproduced identity, locate its earliest accessible source, and record the original parameter restrictions.

title: Varying the numerator k
connection: Study k/n=1/x+1/y+1/z for neighboring fixed k and compare which constructions persist at k=4.
why: Changing k can isolate features specific to four from those common to three-term Egyptian fractions.
first_step: Derive the residual factor equation for k=3,4,5 and compare congruence conditions for the same x ansatz.

title: Two-term and four-term boundary cases
connection: Compare the rigid two-term equation and more flexible four-term constructions with the three-term target.
why: A controlled bridge might identify the exact extra degree of freedom that must be eliminated.
first_step: Start from an explicit four-term identity and solve the exact condition under which two terms merge to one.

title: Distinct-denominator variants
connection: Separate certificates with repeated denominators from those with three distinct denominators and compare their construction mechanisms.
why: Repeated terms form special algebraic slices that might seed perturbative identities.
first_step: Classify the x=y and y=z cases exactly, then search one-parameter deformations preserving integrality.

title: Primitive-to-scaled transfer
connection: Track how primitive denominator shapes generate certificates for composite n and which shapes first appear at prime n.
why: This may reveal composition laws without confusing the easy scaling direction with a converse.
first_step: Canonicalize triples by their common gcd and map the resulting primitive shapes to the reduced fraction they represent.

title: Beyond polynomial parametrizations
connection: Explore rational, recurrent, floor-based, and piecewise arithmetic witness formulas as genuinely different representation classes.
why: A limitation of one formula class need not rule out another, and each class has explicit verification obligations.
first_step: Write one toy certificate rule in each representation class and list exactly how its identity and domain would be proved.

title: A precise question for an outside specialist
connection: Translate one ES subproblem into the native language of a finite-group, algorithmic-number-theory, or dynamics expert.
why: A sharply bounded lemma is more actionable than asking someone to solve the whole conjecture.
first_step: Draft a one-page question about bounded subset products hitting a specified residue, with a small worked ES example and no claim of equivalence beyond the derived map.
